posts.title: House Intelligence
posts.hook: A history of house music, told through its records, its machines and the people who danced first.
posts.caption:
House didn't start in a studio. It started on dancefloors: the Loft, the Warehouse, the Music Box, the Paradise Garage, built by Black, Latino and queer crowds who kept disco alive after radio declared it dead.

House Intelligence is an open archive of that story: 82 records mapped like a metro, from MFSB in 1973 to amapiano in 2024. For each one, how it was built, who made it, which club it belonged to, and why it still matters.

One record a post, starting now.

posts.hook: From now on, anyone with an 808 can make a record.
posts.caption:
On and On · Jesse Saunders · Chicago, 1984

The record most often cited as the first house 12" ever pressed. A looped TR-808, a bouncing synth bass, a vocal pared down to a mantra.

The story is better than the music: Saunders rebuilt from memory a bootleg edit he used to play out and that had been stolen from him. House begins as a home-made copy of a vanished record.

The template was set: a DJ, a second-hand machine, an independent pressing (Larry Sherman's plant, the future home of Trax) and a straight line to the local record shops.

120 BPM · 5A · Energy 6/10

posts.hook: A bass machine designed to back up guitarists, turned into a voice that squeals and chokes.
posts.caption:
Acid Tracks · Phuture · Chicago, 1987

DJ Pierre, Earl "Spanky" Smith Jr. and Herb J got hold of a second-hand Roland TB-303 without knowing how to use it. The accident became the method: Spanky programmed, Pierre twisted the cutoff and resonance until that sound appeared.

Ron Hardy played the tape several times in one night at the Music Box. The crowd rejected it, then demanded it. The name "acid" came from a rumour that the DJ was spiking the water.

Acid was born in a Black and gay club. Once it crossed the Atlantic, the smiley partly erased where it came from.

120 BPM · 10A · TB-303 + TR-707

posts.hook: Proof that Chicago house could be tender and sensual.
posts.caption:
Your Love · Jamie Principle · Chicago, 1986

An endlessly cycling arpeggio, a minimal bassline and an almost whispered vocal. Jamie Principle wrote it; Frankie Knuckles played it from tape in clubs for over a year before it came out on Persona in April 1986. Trax reissued it in 1987, credited to Knuckles.

That is how Chicago worked: the DJ is the first broadcaster, the record comes later.

Knuckles, the Godfather of House, was a Black gay DJ from the Bronx and the Continental Baths. "Your Love" is one of the founding love songs of queer house.

120 BPM · 1A · Energy 6/10

posts.hook: The club that gave house its name.
posts.caption:
The Warehouse · Chicago · 1977–1982

Frankie Knuckles played here from 1977 until November 1982, when he left for the Power Plant. The crowd was mostly Black and gay.

Where does the word "house" come from? Three versions still compete: a sign Knuckles saw, the "As heard at the Warehouse" bins at the Importes Etc. record shop, or simply a generic name for that kind of disco.

Line 1 · Chicago & Acid. Listen: Love Is the Message (MFSB, 1973) · Your Love (Jamie Principle, 1986)

posts.hook: The bridge between house and techno: orchestral emotion carried by the machine.
posts.caption:
Strings of Life · Rhythim Is Rhythim · Detroit, 1987

Sampled strings and a piano improvisation by Michael James, cut into syncopated riffs over a relentless 909. No conventional bassline, so the tension never resolves: an orchestra in free fall.

Derrick May saw the machine as a way out of a city the car industry had left behind. In Europe, the record became a rave anthem.

The techno story often forgets its queer debts, starting with Ken Collier, the Black gay Detroit DJ whose sets schooled a whole generation.

125 BPM · 4B · Energy 9/10

posts.title: TR-909
posts.hook: Too expensive, unconvincing, sold off cheap. Then it became the unit of measure.
posts.caption:
Roland TR-909 · 1983

Roland built it to succeed the 808, with sampled cymbals and MIDI sync. At launch it was judged too expensive and not realistic enough, and it was sold off cheap.

That is how it reached Detroit and Chicago. Its punchy kick became the unit of measure of house and techno, and its open hi-hat defined the off-beat of the dancefloor.

Heard on: Strings of Life · Can You Feel It · Big Fun · Da Funk · Frozen (Victor Calderone)

In The Booth, the pulse plays each record at its exact tempo with a 909 kick.

posts.hook: Every “ha” calls for a pose, every crash for a dip.
posts.caption:
The Ha Dance · Masters At Work · New York, 1991

A "ha!" sampled from Trading Places, a crash cymbal, a nervy rhythm. Louie Vega and Kenny "Dope" Gonzalez made an instrumental; ballroom made it a choreography. The crash on the fourth beat became the cue for vogue femme's dip.

The sample comes from a scene full of blackface and slurs. Black and Latina, queer and trans ballroom turned it around, and has been reissuing and remixing it for more than thirty years.

122 BPM · 4A · SP-1200 + MPC60

posts.hook: Ballroom was here before house. Then they found each other.
posts.caption:
Ballroom & Voguing · 1920s–

Ballroom predates house: its roots go back to the Harlem Renaissance. "Old Way" took hold in the 1980s (House of LaBeija, House of Corey), "New Way" in the early 1990s.

The link with house came through the Sound Factory (1989–1995) and The Ha Dance (1991): every "ha" calls for a pose.

Listen: You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real) · Vogue · The Ha Dance · Gypsy Woman · Show Me Love

Lines 2 and 7 on the house metro map.

posts.hook: Three tempos, three ways to move. Press play in The Booth and feel the difference.
posts.foot: Focalistic & Vigro Deep · Marshall Jefferson · Artful Dodger
posts.caption:
Same pulse, three bodies.

113 BPM: Ke Star (Focalistic & Vigro Deep, 2020). Amapiano sways more than it pushes; the log drum carries the melody.
121 BPM: Move Your Body (Marshall Jefferson, 1986). Chicago jack, the house anthem.
132 BPM: Re-Rewind (Artful Dodger feat. Craig David, 1999). UK garage, skipping on a 2-step.

In The Booth, a small drum machine plays each record's exact tempo with a 909 kick, an 808 sub or a 303 line, and suggests the next record by Camelot key and BPM, like a DJ would.

posts.hook: House can slow down without losing its power to move a floor.
posts.caption:
Ke Star · Focalistic & Vigro Deep · Pretoria, 2020

The log drum, a percussive bass with a signature glide, carries the melody. Constant shakers, a discreet kick, Focalistic's Sepitori flow floating on top. The groove is horizontal.

Vigro Deep, a teenage producer from Mabopane, belongs to the generation that shaped amapiano on FL Studio in Gauteng's townships. Born at neighbourhood parties, in taxis and taverns, the genre was pushed across the continent by the 2020 lockdown.

Forty years after Chicago, the same question: who holds the keys to house? Black youth, this time in Africa.

113 BPM · 5A · Log drum

posts.hook: A single preset colour is enough to define a decade.
posts.caption:
Show Me Love (StoneBridge Club Mix) · Robin S · New York, 1992

Swedish remixer StoneBridge threw out the original production and kept the voice: an organ bass from a Korg M1 preset, a dry kick, and Robin S soaring over it. That M1 organ became one of the sounds of the 90s.

The remix went global in 1993 and has been sampled and remixed for thirty years since. On gay dancefloors and in ballroom, it is the gospel diva voice par excellence.

122 BPM · 10A · Korg M1

posts.hook: House went back to Africa, and came back rewritten.
posts.caption:
Line 8 · Africas

Afro House → Gqom → Amapiano

South African house was born in Hillbrow and Pretoria in the late 1980s, next to kwaito. In Durban, gqom broke the kick and travelled by taxi and WhatsApp. In Gauteng, amapiano slowed everything down and gave the melody to the log drum.

House there is mass popular music, not a niche.

Listen: Township Funk · Superman · Ice Drop · Ke Star · Water · Tshwala Bam

posts.hook: All of house descends from this break.
posts.caption:
Love Is the Message · MFSB · Philadelphia, 1973

A message for today, and the record where it all begins.

Gamble & Huff's studio orchestra: silky strings, horns and a bass-and-drums groove that stands on its own. The long instrumental break became DJs' raw material, looped on two decks for minutes on end. That loop, as a place of collective trance, is what house is made of.

An anthem of David Mancuso's Loft and of 1970s New York's Black and Latino gay dancefloors, where its promise of universal love became the dancefloor's own.

118 BPM · 4A · Energy 6/10

posts.title: TR-808
posts.hook: It sounded like no real drum kit. That was the point.
posts.caption:
Roland TR-808 · 1980

Roland wanted a programmable, "realistic" drum kit to back musicians in rehearsal. It sounded like no real drums and sold poorly.

Resold cheap on the second-hand market, it fell into the hands of New York electro, hip-hop and then Chicago's first house producers. Its kick, a deep sine wave with a long decay, doubles as a bassline: the 808 sub.

Heard on: On and On · Don't Make Me Wait · Voodoo Ray · Yo Yo Get Funky!

Discontinued after a few years, it became one of the most sampled machines in history.

posts.hook: "Brothers, sisters, one day we will be free."
posts.caption:
Promised Land · Joe Smooth · Chicago, 1987

The last record of the year: luminous piano chords, a gospel progression and a lyric of hope. House as a civil-rights hymn.

Joe Smooth, a Chicago DJ schooled in soul and gospel, wrote a political anthem in a genre said to be apolitical. Then the "promised land" of a Black and queer scene became the utopia of British ravers in 1988 and 1989, a transfer of meaning at the heart of house history.

120 BPM · 3B · Energy 7/10

posts.hook: A scene naming itself, and giving itself an anthem.
posts.caption:
Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem) · Marshall Jefferson · Chicago, 1986

Hammered piano chords over a rigid drum-machine pattern, an octave bassline and Curtis McClain's church-born vocal. The birth certificate of piano house.

Jefferson worked at the post office and bought his machines on credit, building tracks part by part. Ron Hardy played it at the Music Box, Frankie Knuckles at the Power Plant. "Gotta have house music, all night long": for a Black, gay, working-class crowd, a secular church.

121 BPM · 8B · TR-707

posts.hook: Emotion through chords, not effects.
posts.caption:
Can You Feel It · Mr. Fingers · Chicago, 1986

Warm pads, a round bassline and almost no variation for seven minutes. Depth comes from restraint. This is the template for all deep house.

Larry Heard was a jazz-fusion drummer, and he composes as a harmonist, with sevenths and ninths. Later versions carry Chuck Roberts's sermon: "In the beginning there was Jack." House as a feeling, a theology of belonging born in Black gay clubs.

120 BPM · 6A · TR-909 + Juno-60

posts.title: MPC60
posts.hook: Sixteen pads and a swing setting that made loops feel human.
posts.caption:
Akai MPC60 · 1988

Designed with Roger Linn as a complete studio in a box: sampling, sequencing and playable pads.

The velocity-sensitive pads and Linn's quantise swing gave loops a human groove. Hip-hop seized it first, then New York garage and house producers who played samples like percussion. Later, UK garage.

Heard on: The Ha Dance (Masters At Work, 1991)

"MPC swing" is now a setting of its own in modern music software.

posts.hook: The dancefloor as a church. The word "garage" comes from here.
posts.caption:
Paradise Garage · New York · 1977–1987

At 84 King Street, Larry Levan turned the dancefloor into a church for a mostly gay Black and Latino crowd: soul, gospel, dub effects and a legendary sound system.

Garage house took its name from this room.

Listen: Love Is the Message · Love Sensation · Is It All Over My Face · Don't Make Me Wait

posts.hook: Global pop at the service of the New York queer dancefloor.
posts.caption:
Frozen (Victor Calderone Extended Club Mix) · Madonna · New York, 1998

Calderone turns a dark ballad into a tribal cathedral: cascading toms, rolling percussion, long builds and dramatic breakdowns. Madonna's voice becomes an incantation over a carpet of drums.

Late-90s Manhattan: Twilo, Roxy, Sound Factory and the circuit parties, a post-AIDS culture of the body, the night and collective survival. Madonna had borrowed vogue from ballroom in 1990; here the loop closes.

posts.hook: Faster than Chicago, yet looser.
posts.caption:
Re-Rewind (The Crowd Say Bo Selecta) · Artful Dodger feat. Craig David · Southampton, 1999

Two-step: the kick skips beats, the snare is syncopated, the hats shuffle and the bass bounces. Craig David's R&B vocal dances on top. Mix it after a 121 BPM Chicago record and you feel the shift.

UK garage was Sunday sessions, pirate radio and MCs, with a sharp dress code. A Black British working-class culture that gave birth to grime and dubstep, and that police targeted through Form 696.

132 BPM · 2A · Energy 8/10

posts.hook: House changes as it travels: slowed down, saturated, pop.
posts.caption:
Da Funk · Daft Punk · Paris, 1995

A distorted, filtered synth-bass riff halfway between funk and acid, over a compressed 909. At 111 BPM the groove is heavy, closer to G-funk than to Chicago.

It first came out on Soma, Slam's Glasgow label, before Virgin signed the duo. The French Touch was recognised in London before Paris. And the Paris scene crystallised at the Respect nights at Queen, a gay club on the Champs-Élysées; their tour was called "Respect Is Burning".

posts.hook: One technical gesture, repeated to ecstasy.
posts.caption:
Music Sounds Better With You · Stardust · Paris, 1998

A loop from Chaka Khan's "Fate" (1981) runs through a filter that opens and closes over a four-to-the-floor kick, with Benjamin Diamond singing on top. The whole track rests on the filter's breathing.

Thomas Bangalter, Alan Braxe and Benjamin Diamond released only one record under this name. Filter house turned the disco of 1970s Black and gay dancefloors into raw material for a wider audience: homage or appropriation, depending on how you hear it.

124 BPM · 11B · Energy 7/10

Bright vocal house, a round bassline and Hadiya George's soul voice: Chicago house rewritten for 2022.

posts.hook: The first great acid classic made outside the United States.
posts.caption:
Voodoo Ray · A Guy Called Gerald · Manchester, 1988

Gerald Simpson, a young Black Mancunian, made it in his bedroom on second-hand gear: a more melodic 303 than Phuture's, a light 808 groove and a voice chopped into abstraction. Proof that house had become a language others could speak.

An anthem of 1988's Second Summer of Love: the Haçienda, warehouse parties, then the orbital raves around the M25, until the 1994 Criminal Justice Act.

122 BPM · 9A · TB-303 + TR-808

posts.hook: Britain made house its own, and never stopped mutating it.
posts.caption:
Line 4 · UK Sound System & Bass

Sound systems → Shoom & Haçienda → Bleep → Hardcore & Jungle → UK Garage → Dubstep → Chart house

Before acid house, Britain danced to Jamaican sound systems and jazz-funk all-dayers. It kept that cult of sub-bass through every mutation: bleep in Sheffield, jungle, 2-step, dubstep in Croydon, and in 2013 house at the top of the charts.

Listen: Keep On Movin' · Voodoo Ray · LFO · Re-Rewind · Midnight Request Line · White Noise

posts.hook: House returning to Africa, rewritten rather than imported.
posts.caption:
Superman · Black Coffee feat. Bucie · Durban / Johannesburg, 2009

Woody, polyrhythmic percussion, melancholic pads and Bucie's voice. The groove is restrained, almost deep, but it breathes differently from American four-to-the-floor.

Nathi "Black Coffee" Maphumulo grew up in Umlazi. In 1990 he was injured when a car ploughed into a crowd celebrating Mandela's release, and lost most of the use of his left arm. He learned to mix one-handed. In South Africa, this was the hit of a generation.

120 BPM · 3A · Energy 5/10

posts.title: TB-303
posts.hook: Built to replace a bass player. It started to talk instead.
posts.caption:
Roland TB-303 · 1981

Roland made it for guitarists rehearsing alone. It sounded nothing like an electric bass, flopped, and was discontinued within a few years.

In Chicago, Phuture twisted the cutoff, resonance, accent and slide live. The bass started to "talk", and acid house was born from that accident. Its programming is so counter-intuitive that many famous patterns came from mistakes.

Heard on: Acid Tracks · Voodoo Ray · Da Funk

posts.hook: A dancefloor hit that speaks about the street.
posts.caption:
Gypsy Woman (She's Homeless) · Crystal Waters · Baltimore, 1991

An organ riff, a dry kick and the famous "la da dee la dee da". Crystal Waters, a poet and civil servant, wrote a song about a homeless woman, and the Basement Boys produced it in the wake of New York garage.

A worldwide hit about urban poverty over a euphoric groove. In ballroom, the "la da dee" became a vogue classic, reused in remix after remix.

122 BPM · 11A · Energy 7/10
